title: GZIP file format specification version 4.3
summary: Defines the gzip file format, a lossless compressed data format compatible with the widely used gzip utility. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Like vacuum-packing clothes to take up less space in a suitcase. You unpack them later and everything is still the same.

questions: what is the gzip file format
how does the gzip header work
what are the gzip magic bytes
subtitle: The file format behind the gzip utility: members with a header, deflate data and a CRC-32 trailer.

tldr.problem: A lossless compressed format was needed that is portable across systems, works on streams with bounded memory, compresses well, avoids patents, and stays compatible with the widely used gzip utility.
tldr.mechanism: A gzip file is a series of members. Each has a header (magic bytes, method, flags, modification time, OS, optional fields), deflate-compressed blocks, and an 8-byte trailer with CRC32 and ISIZE.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is informational. It documents the format of the existing gzip utility so independent implementations can read and write it.

today: RFC 1952 is an Informational RFC and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Goals of the gzip Format
sections.content:
RFC 1952 defines a lossless compressed data format that is independent of CPU type, operating system, file system and character set. It can compress or decompress a data stream using only an a priori bounded amount of intermediate storage, so it suits Unix filters and data communications.

It aims to compress with efficiency comparable to the best general-purpose methods of the time, and considerably better than the compress program. It can be implemented without patent problems, and it is compatible with the files produced by the existing gzip utility. It does not try to provide random access, or to beat specialized algorithms on specialized data.
sections.eli5: The goal is a squeezing method that works everywhere, shrinks things well, and can still be opened by the program people already use.

sections.title: Members and the Fixed Header
sections.content:
A gzip file is a series of members (compressed data sets) placed one after another with nothing in between. Each member starts with a 10-byte fixed header: ID1 and ID2 (always 31 and 139, that is 0x1f and 0x8b), CM (compression method), FLG (flags), a 4-byte MTIME, XFL and OS.

CM = 8 means deflate; values 0 to 7 are reserved. MTIME is the modification time of the original file in Unix format (seconds since 00:00:00 GMT, Jan. 1, 1970), and 0 means no time stamp is available. For deflate, XFL = 2 means maximum compression and XFL = 4 means the fastest algorithm. OS names the file system on which compression took place, with 255 meaning unknown.

Multi-byte numbers are stored least-significant byte first, the opposite of the byte order used by RFC 1950.
sections.eli5: Each pack begins with a fixed label: a secret handshake that says this is a gzip pack, how it was squeezed, when the original was last changed, and what kind of computer made it.

sections.title: Optional Header Fields
sections.content:
Bits of FLG turn on optional parts that follow the fixed header: FEXTRA (an extra field of XLEN bytes), FNAME (the original file name, zero-terminated), FCOMMENT (a zero-terminated comment for humans) and FHCRC (a 2-byte CRC16 of the header). FTEXT is an optional hint that the file is probably ASCII text. Bits 5 to 7 are reserved and must be zero.

File names and comments must use ISO 8859-1 (Latin-1) characters. The name has directory components removed. The extra field is a series of subfields, each with a two-byte ID (SI1, SI2), a 2-byte LEN and data. The only ID defined in the RFC is A P for Apollo file type information, and IDs with SI2 = 0 are reserved.
sections.eli5: The label can have extra stickers: the original file name, a note, or a little custom tag. A flag tells the reader which stickers are there.

sections.title: Compressed Data and Trailer
sections.content:
After the header comes the compressed blocks, which for method 8 use the deflate format documented in a separate specification. Each member ends with an 8-byte trailer. CRC32 is a cyclic redundancy check of the uncompressed data, computed as in ISO 3309 and ITU-T V.42. ISIZE is the size of the original data modulo 2^32.

The sample code in the appendix computes the CRC with a table of CRCs of all 8-bit messages. The appendices are not part of the specification and are not relevant to compliance.
sections.eli5: At the end of each pack are two numbers: a check value that spots damage, and the size of the original, so you can tell if something is missing.

sections.title: Compliance Rules
sections.content:
A compliant compressor must produce correct ID1, ID2, CM, CRC32 and ISIZE. It may use defaults for the rest of the fixed header (255 for OS, 0 for the others) and must set reserved bits to zero.

A compliant decompressor must check ID1, ID2 and CM and report an error if any is wrong. It must examine FEXTRA/XLEN, FNAME, FCOMMENT and FHCRC at least well enough to skip them. It may ignore FTEXT and OS. It must report an error if any reserved bit is non-zero, since that bit could signal a new field that would make later data be misread.
sections.eli5: Anyone writing a pack must fill in the key parts correctly. Anyone opening one must check the secret handshake and refuse packs with unknown markings.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Compression removes redundancy, so any corruption of compressed data is likely to have severe effects and be difficult to correct. Uncompressed text will probably still be readable despite some corrupted bytes. The RFC recommends that systems using this format provide some means of validating the integrity of the data, such as setting and checking the CRC-32 value.
sections.eli5: A squeezed-up suitcase is harder to fix if something tears, so it is wise to check the contents when you unpack.

fields.desc: Extra flags for the compression method.
